newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma economy still has long way to go, IMF says.
newsitem.headline: Burma economy still has long way to go, IMF says.

text.p: Burma's economy is still suffering from serious macroeconomic problems and the legacy of more than a quarter century of central planning, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
In a report to be presented to Burma's military government on Wednesday, the IMF said although tentative steps had been taken toward liberalising the economy, serious problems remained.
The body said the government needed to adopt a sweeping reform programme to set the economy back on track.

Since seizing power in 1988, Burma's military State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) has been trying to revive the economy, which suffered badly during 26 years of socialist rule and isolationist policies of former leader General Ne Win.

"Myanmar (Burma) has made limited progress toward achieving the goal of a more market-oriented economy," said the report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters. "A number of critical structural defects, however, have not yet been addressed."

"The opaque policy environment, together with the highly distorted exchange market and heavy government intervention throughout the economy, have adversely affected economic efficiency and macroeconomic conditions," it said.

Although real gross domestic product growth has averaged eight percent over the past four years, the IMF said it must be viewed against previous large declines. It said real income per capita had only recovered to its level of a decade ago.
"Recent data...present a more mixed picture with increasing signs of strain," the report said.
It cited an expected slowdown in growth in 1996/97, lower agricultural output and falling exports which add to the problem of dwindling foreign reserves.

"The persistent delay in undertaking economic reforms has prevented Myanmar from realising its full economic potential or substantially raising the living standards of the population," the report said.

"The macroeconomic situation has taken a marked turn for the worse since April 1996. Foreign exchange reserves have fallen sharply, the exchange rate in the parallel market depreciated by 40 percent in six months and inflation has accelerated."

The IMF repeated a previous call for a "one-shot" devaluation of the kyat currency, which is officially set at about six to the U.S. dollar. On the parallel market one dollar buys about 160-165 kyats.

"An adjustment of the official exchange rate to a market clearing level...is a prerequisite for the entire reform process," the report said. "These measures need to be complemented by a wide range of structural reforms."
"Without such a change in policies, growth would fall well short of potential, inflation would remain high and external imbalances would worsen."
The report said Burmese authorities see many of the current problems, especially the low foreign reserves, to be transitory.

"They noted that earnings of $300-$400 million per year from exports of natural gas are expected from mid-1998, which would allow the build-up of an adequate reserve cushion and provide more conducive circumstances under which to implement the recommended fundamental reforms," it said.

But the IMF said most of the foreign exchange earnings from the exports during the first three years of production would be absorbed as the equity contribution to the joint venture with French, U.S. and Thai partners and no revenues would accrue to Burma until the turn of the century.
